title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation fraud in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a convincing interview featuring two real, named public figures, a finance journalist and a central bank governor, in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated exchange included realistic narrative detail, a dramatised walkout, and the apparent authority of recognisable names. The failure mode is synthetic disinformation deployed at scale: AI tools lowering the production cost of fraudulent content enough that scammers can generate and distribute it faster than regulators can remove it.

The fraud happened entirely outside any legitimate deployment pipeline. No licensed institution, platform moderator, or editorial check was in the loop. Catching it would have required either pre-publication content authentication, rapid takedown systems, or audiences trained to verify licensing credentials independently rather than treating polished presentation as a signal of legitimacy.

What is not established is the identity of the operators behind Boulder Sparhaven, the precise AI tools used to generate the content, or the total financial harm caused to investors. ASIC's figures describe the broader trend of AI-assisted investment scams rather than findings specific to this single incident.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featuring ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock was designed to promote Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The fabricated interview depicted them discussing the platform in an increasingly heated exchange that ended with Bullock walking out. This type of scam is becoming more common as artificial intelligence makes fraudulent content more convincing and difficult to detect.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports a significant surge in AI-generated investment scams, removing 19,400 scams last year, up 182 percent. Phishing scams increased 279 percent while fake investment platforms jumped 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most commonly impersonated Australians. ASIC recommends prospective investors verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through their public registers and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
